title: When Dinosaurs Ruled
subtitle: Giants, fossils, the asteroid, and the dinosaurs still alive today
subject: Earth

p: Look out the window. If you can see a sparrow, a crow or a pigeon, you are looking at a dinosaur. That is not a joke. Birds are living dinosaurs, as surely as you are a mammal.

The big ones are gone. The last Tyrannosaurus died 66 million years ago. But their small, feathered cousins kept going, and today there are about 11,000 kinds of them. This book is about the giants, how we know about them, and how a few of them survived.
pages.cap: A sauropod walks through a forest 150 million years ago.
pages.fact: Did you know? Tests on protein from a T. rex bone showed it is closer to chickens and ostriches than to any alligator or lizard.

pages.h: A very, very long time ago
p: Dinosaurs first appeared about 230 million years ago and ruled the land for about 165 million years. Humans like us have been around for 300,000 years. That is less than a fifth of one percent of the dinosaur age.

How long is 66 million years, the time since the last big dinosaur? If you counted one number every second, day and night, never stopping, you would reach 66 million after more than two years. Dinosaurs did not live long ago. They lived unimaginably long ago.
pages.cap: The dinosaur age lasted 500 times longer than humans have existed.
pages.fact: Did you know? T. rex lived closer in time to you than to Stegosaurus. The gap between those two dinosaurs was 84 million years.

pages.h: Three chapters of the dinosaur age
p: Scientists split the dinosaur age into three periods. The Triassic, from 252 to 201 million years ago, was hot and dry. All the land was joined in one giant continent called Pangaea. The first dinosaurs were small and quick, about the size of a dog.

The Jurassic, 201 to 145 million years ago, was wetter and greener. The continents began to split apart and the giant long-necked dinosaurs appeared. The Cretaceous, 145 to 66 million years ago, brought flowering plants, horned dinosaurs and the biggest meat-eaters of all.
pages.cap: As the plates drifted apart, dinosaurs on each continent grew different.
pages.fact: Did you know? In the Triassic, you could have walked from Canada to Africa without crossing an ocean.

pages.why: Birds grew from small feathered dinosaurs. Crocodiles are cousins, and lizards are more distant relatives.

pages.h: The biggest animals to ever walk
p: Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan were long-necked plant-eaters that lived in what is now Argentina about 95 million years ago. Patagotitan stretched about 37 m from nose to tail tip, longer than three school buses parked end to end. It weighed around 57 tonnes, as much as 10 African elephants.
Nothing that heavy has walked on land since. Its heart had to pump blood up a neck more than 10 m tall. Each footprint was wide enough for you to lie down in.
pages.cap: Twenty-eight of you, lying head to toe, would just about match one Patagotitan.
pages.fact: Did you know? A sauropod could swallow 1,000 kg of leaves in a single day without chewing. Its huge gut did the work instead.

p: Not every dinosaur was a giant. Compsognathus was the size of a chicken, about 1 m long including a thin tail, and weighed around 3 kg. It chased lizards and insects on quick little legs.

Microraptor was even smaller, under 1 kg, and had long feathers on all four limbs. It could glide from tree to tree. In fact most dinosaurs were far smaller than the famous giants. Small bones break and rot easily, so we probably still have not found the tiniest ones.
pages.cap: Microraptor's feathered wings and legs caught the air like a glider.
pages.fact: Did you know? The smallest dinosaur alive today is the bee hummingbird. It weighs about 2 g, about the same as a dime.

p: Tyrannosaurus rex was about 12 m long, 4 m tall at the hips, and weighed about 8 tonnes, as much as a loaded truck. Its skull alone was 1.5 m long. Its biggest teeth were 30 cm from tip to root, as long as a ruler, and shaped like thick bananas for crushing bone.
Scientists measured its bite at about 35,000 newtons. That is like having a 3.5 tonne weight pressing on one tooth. Its arms were tiny, but each could still lift more than 100 kg.
pages.cap: A T. rex skeleton: huge skull, strong legs, small arms.
pages.fact: Did you know? T. rex teenagers grew about 2 kg every day for several years, like adding a house cat to their body every two days.

p: In films, T. rex sprints after cars. Real T. rex probably could not. Computer models of its leg bones and muscles suggest a top speed of around 20 to 25 km per hour. Faster than that and its own 8 tonne body would have broken its legs.

A fast 8-year-old sprints at about 15 km per hour. So no, you probably could not outrun it over a short dash. But T. rex walked at only about 5 km per hour, a gentle stroll. On a bike, you would leave it far behind.
pages.cap: Big dinosaurs walked more than they ran; the biggest could barely run at all.
pages.fact: Did you know? Dinosaur footprint trails let scientists measure walking speed from the distance between steps.

pages.h: A dinosaur with a brain the size of a hot dog
p: Stegosaurus weighed about 5 tonnes, as much as a small elephant, but its brain weighed only about 80 g. That is lighter than a hot dog. It did not need to be clever. It needed to eat plants and swing its spiked tail.

Plant-eaters needed armour. Triceratops, 9 m long, had two brow horns over 1 m long and a bony frill behind its head. Ankylosaurus was a walking tank, covered in bony plates, with a tail club that could smash a leg bone.

Stegosaurus carried 17 plates along its back and four tail spikes up to 90 cm long. Scientists have found an Allosaurus tail bone with a spike wound in it, so the spikes were used. Parasaurolophus had a hollow 1 m crest that may have honked like a trombone.
pages.cap: Plants fed the giants; the giants fed the hunters. Armour tipped the balance.
pages.fact: Did you know? Triceratops had up to 800 teeth packed in rows, with new ones growing as old ones wore out.

pages.q: About how heavy was Tyrannosaurus rex?
opts: About 8 tonnes, like a loaded truck
About 80 tonnes, like a blue whale
pages.why: T. rex weighed around 8 tonnes. Only the long-necked sauropods came close to whale size.

pages.h: How a bone becomes a fossil
p: Almost every dinosaur that ever lived rotted away without a trace. A fossil needs luck. The animal has to die near water, be buried fast by mud or sand before scavengers finish it, and then lie still for a very long time.

Over thousands of years, water seeps into the bone. Minerals in the water slowly replace the bone, atom by atom, until the bone is stone in the exact shape of the old bone. Then the ground has to rise and wear away so someone can find it. Only about one animal in a million leaves a fossil.
pages.cap: Fossils lie in layers of rock. The deeper the layer, the older the bones.
pages.fact: Did you know? The oldest dinosaur fossils are more than 230 million years old, but the rock around them was once soft river mud.

p: Bones are only one kind of fossil. Footprints pressed into mud and then baked by the sun tell us how dinosaurs walked and whether they travelled in herds. Fossil eggs show us nests. The largest known dinosaur eggs are 60 cm long, about the length of your arm.

Fossil poo, called coprolites, shows what a dinosaur ate. One T. rex coprolite was 44 cm long and packed with crushed bone. Scientists have even found fossil skin, stomach contents and, in a few rare cases, feathers.
pages.cap: Some dinosaur eggs held babies curled up like chicks, ready to hatch.
pages.fact: Did you know? A trail of 5,000 dinosaur footprints was found in one spot in Bolivia, on a wall of rock that was once flat mud.

p: How do we know a fossil is 66 million years old? Rock forms in layers, newest on top. Deeper means older. That gives the order. For exact ages, scientists use tiny amounts of natural radioactive atoms in volcanic ash layers. These atoms change into other atoms at a steady, known speed, like a clock that cannot be stopped.
Measure how much has changed and you get the age. Different labs using different atoms get the same answers, which is how scientists know the clocks are right.
pages.cap: Ash from ancient eruptions makes thin layers that act as date stamps.
pages.fact: Did you know? The word dinosaur was invented in 1842 by Richard Owen. It means terrible lizard, but dinosaurs were not lizards.

pages.h: Try it: dig like a scientist
p: Find out why digging up fossils takes patience.
steps: Put a chocolate chip cookie on a paper towel. The cookie is the rock. The chips are the fossils.
Using only a toothpick, try to dig out each chip without breaking it.
Keep a tally of how many chips you got out whole and how many broke.
Now imagine the cookie is as big as a car and the chips are 2 m bones. Real digs take months.
pages.cap: Scientists use brushes, dental picks and lots of time.
pages.safe: Wash your hands before and after. Eat the cookie only when you are done digging.

p: Some of the best dinosaur fossils in the world come from Alberta. In Dinosaur Provincial Park, more than 40 kinds of dinosaur have been dug from the hills, and new ones are still being found. The Royal Tyrrell Museum in Drumheller holds more than 160,000 fossils.

Alberta was warm and swampy 75 million years ago, with rivers that buried bones quickly. Albertosaurus, a smaller cousin of T. rex, was named after the province. In 2011, miners there found Borealopelta, an armoured dinosaur so well preserved it still has its skin.
pages.cap: Rivers once flowed across Alberta, burying dinosaurs in soft mud.
pages.fact: Did you know? Borealopelta's skin kept traces of its colour. It was reddish brown on top and lighter underneath, like a deer.

p: For 150 years, nobody knew. Artists painted dinosaurs grey or green because that is what big reptiles look like today. Then in 2010, scientists looked at fossil feathers under a powerful microscope and found tiny sacs that once held colour.

Sinosauropteryx, a small feathered dinosaur, turned out to have a ginger and white striped tail. Another, Anchiornis, was black and grey with a red crest on its head. Most dinosaurs still keep their colours secret, and scientists disagree about how much we can trust these tiny clues.
pages.cap: Like a butterfly's wing, feather colour comes from tiny structures we can still find in fossils.
pages.fact: Did you know? The same colour sacs in your hair, called melanosomes, decide whether you are blonde, red-haired or dark-haired.

pages.why: Coprolites are fossilized droppings. They show scientists exactly what a dinosaur ate.

p: Sixty-six million years ago, a rock about 10 km wide, taller than Mount Everest, came out of space at about 20 km per second. It hit the sea near what is now Chicxulub, Mexico, and punched a crater 180 km across.

The blast threw melted rock around the world. Forests caught fire. Giant waves rolled across the oceans. Then dust and soot filled the sky and blocked the Sun for years. Plants died, so plant-eaters starved, so meat-eaters starved. About three out of every four kinds of life on Earth vanished.
pages.cap: The asteroid hit with the force of billions of bombs.
pages.fact: Did you know? A thin layer of a rare metal called iridium, common in asteroids, is found in rocks of exactly that age all around the world.

p: Small animals had the best chance. Mammals the size of rats could hide in burrows and eat seeds and insects. Crocodiles and turtles could wait in cold water. Small birds with beaks could crack seeds that lay in the ground for years after the forests burned.

Some scientists think giant volcanoes in India, which had already been pouring out gas for hundreds of thousands of years, made things worse. Most agree the asteroid struck the final blow. Without it, there might be no people. Mammals only grew large after the dinosaurs left.
pages.cap: Small survivors: the tiniest creatures made it through the dark years.
pages.fact: Did you know? Some ferns were among the first plants to come back, and a spike of fern spores marks the year of the disaster in rocks.

p: Birds have hollow bones, scaly feet, feathers, a wishbone and three main toes, exactly like Velociraptor. They lay hard-shelled eggs and sit on them. Many dinosaurs did too. The dinosaurs never died out. They just got small and took to the sky.

Forget the movie version. Real Velociraptor was the size of a turkey, about 2 m long including its stiff tail, and weighed around 15 kg. In 2007, scientists found bumps on its arm bone where big feathers once attached, just like the bumps on a bird's wing bone.

It hunted in the deserts of Mongolia 75 million years ago, using a 7 cm curved claw on each foot to pin prey down. One famous fossil shows a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops locked together in a fight, buried by a collapsing sand dune.
pages.cap: Hunters and hunted: a Velociraptor fossil still grips its prey.
pages.fact: Did you know? Archaeopteryx, from 150 million years ago, had feathers and wings but also teeth, claws on its wings and a long bony tail.

p: Some famous ancient animals are not dinosaurs at all. Pterosaurs flew on skin wings, and the biggest had a wingspan of 10 m, like a small plane. They were cousins, not dinosaurs. Plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs swam the seas with flippers. Also cousins.

Dimetrodon, with its big sail, lived 50 million years before the first dinosaur and was closer to mammals than to dinosaurs. The rule is simple. A dinosaur walked on land with its legs straight under its body, like a horse, not sprawled out to the sides like a crocodile.
pages.cap: Sea reptiles ruled the water while dinosaurs ruled the land.
pages.fact: Did you know? Mary Anning, a fossil hunter in England, dug out the first complete ichthyosaur skeleton known to science in 1812, when she was 12 years old.

pages.why: The asteroid struck 66 million years ago and ended the age of big dinosaurs. Humans came 65 million years later.

p: Numbers in a book feel small. Pace out the real thing.
steps: Find a long hallway, gym or sidewalk. Take a measuring tape or a metre stick.
Measure 12 m and put a shoe at each end. That is one T. rex, nose to tail.
Measure 2 m. That is a Velociraptor. Stand inside it.
Now try 37 m for Patagotitan. You may need to go outside.
Lie down head to toe with friends to see how many of you fit in each dinosaur.
pages.cap: A T. rex was six Velociraptors long.
pages.safe: Measure in a safe place away from traffic.

pages.h: What we still do not know
p: New kinds of dinosaur are named almost every week, about 50 a year. Scientists still argue about many things. Were the big dinosaurs warm-blooded like birds, cold-blooded like lizards, or something in between? Most now think in between. Did T. rex have feathers or scales? Skin fossils show scales, but it may have had feathers as a baby.
What sounds did they make? Probably not roars. Birds and crocodiles hum, boom and hiss with closed mouths, so T. rex may have made a deep rumble you felt in your chest.
pages.cap: A deep hum, not a roar, may have been the sound of a T. rex.
pages.fact: Did you know? Over 1,500 kinds of dinosaur have been named so far. Scientists think thousands more are still in the ground.

p: Dinosaurs ruled for 165 million years and still vanished. That is a big lesson. Earth changes, sometimes suddenly, and no creature stays on top forever. The rocks that hold dinosaur bones also hold the story of how life recovers after disaster.

And every time you hear a robin sing or see a goose fly over in a V, you are watching the end of that story, still going. The dinosaurs' great-great-grandchildren are sitting on a wire outside, waiting for you to notice them.
pages.cap: A tree, its birds, and 230 million years of history in one view.
pages.fact: Did you know? There are almost twice as many kinds of bird alive today as there are kinds of mammal.

items: The remains or traces of an ancient living thing, turned to stone over a very long time.
A huge plant-eating dinosaur with a long neck and tail, like Patagotitan.
A dinosaur that walked on two legs, usually a meat-eater, like T. rex and Velociraptor. Birds are theropods.
Gone forever, with no living members left.
A rock from space, from a few metres to hundreds of kilometres wide.
A bowl-shaped hole made when something hits the ground hard.
The last period of the dinosaur age, 145 to 66 million years ago.
A line of fossil footprints left by one walking animal.

qs: If you found a new dinosaur, what would you name it, and what would you want to find out about it first?
The big dinosaurs disappeared and mammals got their chance. Do you think disasters can ever be good for life in the long run?
We cannot ever see a living T. rex. How sure can we be about what it looked like and how it acted?
